externalities-s1.title: A factory upriver: a negative production externality graph

table.caption: An invented market for paper in which each ton made releases fumes that cost nearby residents \$4 per ton (invented data for practice)

externalities-s3.title: Four situations in an invented city
externalities-s3.text: (1) A cement plant's dust settles on cars nearby. (2) Students who get a flu shot also make their classmates less likely to fall ill. (3) A gardener's flower beds, planted for her own business, make the whole street nicer to walk along. (4) Late-night fireworks bought for private parties keep neighbors awake.

items.q: A factory's production pollutes a river used by people downstream. Label the axes and every curve of the externality graph.

why.correct: Price on the vertical axis, Quantity on the horizontal axis. Demand is D = MPB = MSB (no benefit falls on others). Supply is S = MPC, the firms' own cost. MSC lies above S by the external cost per unit.

items.q: On this negative production externality graph, mark the quantity and price the unregulated market produces.

why.correct: Buyers and sellers look only at private benefit and private cost, so the market settles where MPB, the demand curve, meets MPC, the supply curve.

slips.MSC: MSC includes the pollution cost, which the sellers do not pay; the market ignores it.

items.q: On this negative production externality graph, mark the socially efficient quantity and price.

why.correct: Efficiency counts every cost: the efficient point is where MSB, here the demand curve, meets MSC, at a smaller quantity and a higher price than the market's.

items.q: Shade the deadweight loss caused by the negative production externality.

why.correct: Units between the efficient quantity and the market quantity cost society more (MSC) than they are worth (MSB). The deadweight loss is the triangle between MSC and D from the efficient quantity to the market quantity, pointing toward the efficient quantity (region dwl).

slips.ext-cost: That is the total external cost of all the units made. Only the part beyond the efficient quantity is deadweight loss.

items.q: The government places a per-unit tax on the polluting firms equal to the external cost per unit. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: The tax raises each firm's marginal cost by the external cost, so supply shifts up (left) onto MSC. The new equilibrium is the efficient one: a higher price and a smaller quantity.

key.because: a per-unit tax equal to the external cost

slips.D: The tax is paid by the sellers per unit, so it raises their cost: supply shifts, not demand.

items.q: Getting a flu shot also protects the people around you. On this positive consumption externality graph, mark the socially efficient quantity and price.

why.correct: MSB lies above demand (MPB) by the external benefit. The efficient point is where MSB meets MSC, here the supply curve: a larger quantity than the market makes.

items.q: The government gives buyers of flu shots a per-unit subsidy equal to the external benefit. Shift the right curve and mark the new equilibrium.

why.correct: A subsidy to buyers raises what each buyer gains from a shot, so demand shifts right onto MSB. The new equilibrium is the efficient quantity, larger than before, at a higher price received by sellers.

key.because: a per-unit subsidy to buyers equal to the external benefit

slips.S: The subsidy goes to buyers here, so it raises their willingness to pay: demand shifts.

items.q: A beekeeper's bees pollinate nearby orchards for free: a positive production externality. Shade the deadweight loss.

why.correct: MSC lies below S (MPC) by the external benefit, so the market makes less than the efficient quantity, where D meets MSC. The deadweight loss is the triangle between D and MSC from the market quantity to the efficient quantity (region dwl).

items.q: In the graph, which area is the deadweight loss?
options: Areas a, b and c
Area c
Area a
Area b

why.correct: Deadweight loss counts only the units that should not be made, and only the amount by which their MSC exceeds their MSB.
options: Together these are the total external cost of every unit the market makes.
Area c lies between D and S beyond the efficient quantity; it is part of what buyers and sellers gain on those units.
Right: the triangle between MSC and D from the efficient quantity to the market quantity.
Area b is the external cost of units that are worth making.

items.q: In the graph, which area is the total external cost of the quantity the market produces?
options: Areas a, b and c
Area a
Areas b and c
Area b

why.correct: The external cost per unit is the vertical gap between MSC and MPC. Summed over every unit made, it is the whole band out to the market quantity.
options: Right: the band between MSC and S from zero to the market quantity.
Area a is the deadweight loss only.
That leaves out area a, which is also between MSC and S.
That is the external cost of the efficient quantity only.

items.q: In the graph, how do the market quantity and the efficient quantity compare, and why?
options: The market makes less, because pollution lowers demand
They are equal, because the market is competitive
The market makes more, because buyers value the good above its price
The market makes more, because firms ignore the external cost

why.correct: With a negative externality, MSC > MPC, so the market overproduces and charges too low a price.
options: Demand is unchanged; the extra cost falls on people outside the market.
Competition reaches MSB = MSC only when sellers bear every cost.
The overproduction comes from the cost side, not from buyers.
Right: they produce where MPB = MPC, beyond where MSB = MSC.

items.q: Use the table. What are the market quantity and the socially efficient quantity of paper?
options: Market 40 tons; efficient 50 tons
Market 50 tons; efficient 40 tons
Market 50 tons; efficient 50 tons
Market 60 tons; efficient 40 tons

why.correct: The market uses private curves (MPB = MPC); efficiency uses social curves (MSB = MSC).
options: The market ignores the fumes, so it makes more, not less.
Right: MPB = MPC at 50 (\$10), and MSB = MSC at 40 (\$12).
At 50 tons MSC (\$14) is above MSB (\$10).
At 60 tons MPC (\$12) is above MPB (\$8), so the market stops sooner.

items.q: Use the table. What per-unit tax on paper would lead the market to the efficient quantity, in dollars per ton?

why.correct: Set the tax equal to the external cost per unit at the efficient quantity: MSC - MPC at 40 tons = \$12 - \$8 = \$4 per ton. Firms then face the full social cost.

mistakes.why: \$12 is the whole marginal social cost at 40 tons. The tax should add only the part firms ignore: \$12 - \$8.
\$8 is the firms' own marginal cost at 40 tons. The tax equals the gap between MSC and MPC.

items.q: Use the table. Assume the curves are straight lines between the rows. What is the deadweight loss at the market quantity, in dollars per day?

why.correct: Between 40 and 50 tons, MSC is above MSB. At 50 tons the gap is \$14 - \$10 = \$4, and at 40 tons it is zero. DWL = ½ × (50 - 40) × \$4 = \$20.

mistakes.why: \$40 is the rectangle. The gap shrinks to zero at 40 tons, so the area is a triangle: take one half.
\$100 uses all 50 tons as the base. Only the 10 tons beyond the efficient quantity are lost.

items.q: Use the table. With the corrective tax of \$4 per ton, the market makes the efficient quantity. How much tax revenue does the government collect per day, in dollars?

why.correct: Tax revenue = tax × quantity after the tax = \$4 × 40 = \$160.

mistakes.why: \$200 uses the quantity before the tax. Revenue uses the quantity after the tax: 40 tons.

items.q: In the scenario, which situation is a positive consumption externality?
options: (1) the cement dust
(2) the flu shots
(3) the flower beds
(4) the fireworks

why.correct: Sort by two questions: does it help or harm others, and does it come from making the good or from using it?
options: That is a cost from production: a negative production externality.
Right: using (consuming) the shot benefits other people.
That benefit comes from a firm's production: a positive production externality.
That is a cost from consumption: a negative consumption externality.

items.q: In the scenario, for situation (4), how do MSB and MPB compare, and what does the market do?
options: MSB is above MPB, so the market buys too few fireworks
MSC is above MPC, so the market buys too many fireworks
MSB equals MPB, so the market is efficient
MSB is below MPB, so the market buys too many fireworks

why.correct: A negative consumption externality puts MSB below the demand curve (MPB), so the market quantity exceeds the efficient quantity.
options: That would be a benefit to others, not a cost.
The cost comes from using the fireworks, not making them, so it is shown on the benefit side.
The neighbors bear a cost that buyers ignore.
Right: the neighbors' lost sleep is a cost of using the good, so society's benefit is less than the buyers'.

items.q: In the scenario, which policy is matched to the cause of the market failure in situation (2)?
options: A per-unit subsidy to people who get the shot
A per-unit tax on flu shots
A lump-sum payment to clinics whatever number of shots they give
A price ceiling on flu shots below the market price

why.correct: The external benefit comes from consumption, so pay buyers per unit: the subsidy shifts demand to MSB.
options: Right: it raises buyers' benefit to match MSB, so more people get the shot.
A tax would lower the quantity, but the market already makes too few.
A payment that does not depend on the number given does not change the quantity.
A binding ceiling cuts the quantity supplied, moving further from the efficient quantity.

items.q: What is an externality?
options: A good that is sold to buyers in other countries
A cost that a firm pays to its outside suppliers
A cost or benefit of a deal that falls on people outside it
A benefit a buyer gets from a good she pays for

why.correct: Because the third party is not part of the deal, the market ignores the effect, and the quantity is not efficient.
options: That is an export.
A cost the firm pays itself is a private cost.
Right: a third party gains or loses without paying or being paid.
That is a private benefit, already in demand.

items.q: A town charges a polluting factory a fixed fee of \$50,000 a year, whatever it produces. What happens to the factory's output and to the deadweight loss?
options: Output falls to the efficient quantity, removing the deadweight loss
Output rises, because the factory makes more to cover the fee
Output falls, but the deadweight loss rises
Neither changes, because the fee does not change marginal cost

why.correct: To correct an externality, the policy must change the marginal decision: a per-unit tax equal to the external cost. A lump-sum tax changes profit, not output.
options: Only a per-unit tax changes the cost of the last unit and so the quantity.
A fixed fee is paid whatever the output; it gives no reason to make more.
With MC unchanged, output does not change.
Right: a lump-sum tax raises total and average cost, but not MC, so output stays where it was.

items.q: Insulating a home also lowers neighbors' shared heating costs. At the efficient quantity of insulation, a unit's marginal social benefit is \$13 and its marginal private benefit to the buyer is \$10. What per-unit subsidy to buyers corrects the market, in dollars per unit?

why.correct: A corrective (Pigouvian) subsidy equals the external benefit per unit at the efficient quantity: MSB - MPB = \$13 - \$10 = \$3.

mistakes.why: \$13 is the whole social benefit. Buyers already count \$10 of it; the subsidy adds only the external part, \$13 - \$10.
\$23 adds the two benefits. The external benefit is the gap between them.

items.q: Which statement about a negative production externality is correct?
options: The market price is too high and the quantity too low
The market price is too low and the quantity too high
MSC lies below MPC
Demand lies above MSB

why.correct: Negative production externality: MSC > MPC, market Q > efficient Q, market P < efficient P.
options: That is the pattern of a positive production externality.
Right: firms do not pay the external cost, so supply is too far right.
With a negative production externality MSC lies above MPC.
The externality is on the cost side; here demand equals MSB.

items.q: Which policies would move a market with a negative production externality toward the efficient quantity? Select all that apply.
options: A per-unit tax on producers equal to the external cost
A lump-sum tax on each producer
A per-unit subsidy to producers
A per-unit tax on buyers equal to the external cost
A price ceiling below the market price

why.correct: A per-unit tax equal to the external cost, on either side of the market, makes buyers and sellers face the full social cost of the last unit.
options: Right: it shifts supply up to MSC.
It leaves marginal cost, price and quantity unchanged.
That would raise output further.
Right: it lowers demand by the same amount and leads to the same quantity.
It cuts output, but sets a price that does not match MSC; it is not a corrective tax.
